newsitem.title: indonesia: OPINION-Profit-taking March flavour in Jakarta.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-Profit-taking March flavour in Jakarta.

text.p: By Tom Ingles, head of research
PT ING Barings Securities Indonesia

JAKARTA, March 13 - After a spectacular run between December and the end of February, during which time Indonesian stocks, as measured by the JSE Composite Index, rose 24 percent, the market greeted March with some long-awaited profit-taking and the index has retraced some five percent so far this month.
There were a number of external factors behind this correction, including some weakness on Wall Street and the fall-out from the Thai financial system's woes.
However, this was exacerbated by several disappointments locally.

First, one of the cigarette giants, HM Sampoerna, came in with unaudited 1996 profits some 10 percent below expectations, plus some hefty downward revisions to internal earnings projections for 1997 and 1998.

This was folowed by a poor reaction to results released by the recently-privatised state-owned Bank Negara Indonesia . Although the results were comfortably ahead of the IPO forecast, it seems that expectations in some quarters were rather higher.

The market was also hit by revelations that Semen Gresik would be hard pushed to meet consensus forecasts due to a change in the tax treatment of its expenditure on heavy equipment and the reclassification of a number of other profit and loss account items.

The share price of that company has now fallen 25 percent from its high for the year, notwithstanding growing evidence that fears of oversupply within the industry over the next two years are looking increasingly exaggerated.

However, the biggest shock to the market came this week when reports emerged that Bank Indonesia has sought to curb the pace of bank loans again in 1997 and that it intends to impose sanctions on banks whose loans to small enterprises represent less than 20 percent of total outstanding loans.
QUESTION NOW - WHERE DOES THE MARKET GO?
The big question is where the market goes from here, the answer to which is heavily dependent on the upcoming results season.
Although only a handful of companies have made public their 1996 earnings, indications have been received for many more, and there have been few surprises so far.

The final numbers to be reported from the crucial banking sector are unlikely to be a long way from consensus estimates. However, the rate of loan growth experienced is much higher than previously anticipated, with Bank International Indonesia likely to come out with a 45 percent increase, while that of Bank Danamon is up well over 60 percent.

We feel that the market has overreacted to the lending cap announcement. Although loan growth may be less than originally expected, the end-1966 base is much higher in most cases, such that there seems to be no reason to make any downward forecast adjustments.
Add to this the possibility of further margin improvements as any pressure there might have been for lending rates to fall eases, and the outlook for the sector continues to look bright.
RISE IN POLITICAL TEMPERATURES

Although the outcome of the parliamentary election, due May 29, is not in any serious doubt, with the ruling Golkar faction expected to win again with a handsome majority, political temperatures will undoubtedly rise and sporadic outbreaks of violence (albeit none too serious) are a distinct possibility.
In such a climate, investors can be expected increasingly to take to the sidelines and the flow of fresh funds into the market can be expected to shrink.

The economy remains robust (we are forecasting GDP growth this year of 7.6 percent, only a modest decline from last year's 7.7 percent) and inflation remains under control -- in February, inflation fell to just 4.8 percent YoY, its lowest level since 1992.

Bank Indonesia must continue its efforts to control money supply, which continues to grow at a rate uncomfortably close to 30 percent YoY. This has prevented the authorities from taking their feet off the brakes and goes a long way to explaining the re-imposition of limits on bank credit.

However, this will affect mostly the so-called "less productive" sectors -- property (except for lower cost housing) and consumer -- and the export and infrastructure related industries will remain largely unaffected.

Nevertheless there remains considerable liquidity in the market, as evidenced by the most recent 50 basis point cut in the discount rate on short-term money market securities (SBPU). With capital inflows still strong, we see scope for further deposit rate cuts later this year (albeit, not until after the election).

Under this scenario, while it is difficult to expect any significant progress in share prices ahead of the election as investors seek instead to realign their portfolios rather than inject fresh funds, the outlook for the stock market in the second half of the year remains good.

While we abide by our position that the prospects for significant PER expansion are slim so long as the question of the political succession remains (next year sees a presidential election at which incumbent President Suharto is expected to win his seventh five-year term), we are sticking with our end-1997 target index level of 770, representing potential appreciation of almost 15 percent from current levels.
(NOTE-The views expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters).
